newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Election over, short stg, gilt vols slide.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Election over, short stg, gilt vols slide.

text.p: By Lisa Wilson, reporting from LIFFE floor
Implied volatility of short sterling and gilt options traded on LIFFE defied the economic uncertainties wrought by Labour's landslide election victory and headed down on Friday, traders said.
Traders said there were few signs the scale of Labour's win would allow the party to revert back to more traditional tax-and-spend policies.
"The election is out of the way and volatility is coming off," said a British bank trader on the LIFFE floor.
The Labour Party won the British election with a majority of around 180 seats, ending 18 years of a Conservative government.
Reasonable buying of June 93.50 strike calls and selling of December straddles dominated short sterling trade.
At-the-money June volatility ticked down to 9.00/9.70 percent compared with around 10.00 percent on Thursday and 9.63 percent at the open.
June short sterling futures were trading unchanged at 93.37 by 1043 GMT. However,traders said this was partly due to the limited volume.
"There's less business than I would have expected," said a trader at a U.S. house on the LIFFE floor. "The pits are full but the orders aren't there."
Indeed the election seemed to have faded into the background as the market focused on the U.S. non-farm payrolls data due 1230 GMT.
"It's sad but the non-farms are far more important for the market than Tony Blair," said a short-sterling options trader.
In the gilts market, volatility swung wildly but by 1045 GMT was trading down on the day at 7.10 to 7.50 percent, compared with 8.22 percent at the open and 8.06 percent at the prior close.
June 112-00 calls were actively traded and upside call buying and bullish strategy dominated the market.
June gilt futures were up 7/32 at 111-00.

An early attempt to push volatility below 7.0 percent was met with strong resistance as traders said it was too soon to write the uncetainty out of the markets. But some gilts call strikes did trade at volatilities in the 6.9 percent area.

"I'm frankly surprised," said a European options trader. "The issue is that people cannot be sure what Labour is going to do and it was crazy to see vol at 6.9 percent," he said. "To my mind it looks cheap at seven and a half percent."
